newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Danes still to veto EU anti-Cuba move.
newsitem.headline: Danes still to veto EU anti-Cuba move.

text.p: Denmark said on Monday it had had no change of heart and would continue to block a European Union move to combat Washington's anti-Cuba trade policy in its present form.
Danish foreign minister Niels Helveg Petersen, arriving for a meeting of his EU counterparts, said Copenhagen's "legal problems" remained over ways to counter the Helms-Burton Act.

The EU ministers were expected to agree restrictions on Burma in response to what the EU sees as a lack of progress on democracy, to discuss the deteriorating situation in Zaire and to plan the bloc's next moves in the Middle East peace process.
But the row over Cuba was the top item on the agenda.
"We have not come to block the proposals," Petersen said. "We come to seek a solution ... but we cannot agree with it in this form."

Denmark stunned the European Commission and EU countries last week by saying concerns over national sovereignty would prevent it approving laws to counter Washington's Helms-Burton Act, an amalgamation of years of anti-Cuba policy.
The Danish government is currently embroiled in a court case brought by a citizens' group that accuses it of handing too much sovereignty to the EU.

Copenhagen says it cannot go along with EU action based on a catch-all clause in the EU's founding treaties, which is regarded with suspicion by governments wary of ceding too much authority to the bloc.

On Burma, the EU has already agreed in principle to ban visits by ministers and high-level officials to Burma and to refuse visas to members of Rangoon's State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC).
Diplomats said the EU was distressed by the unwillingness of the SLORC to improve its record on human rights and democracy.
Belgian Foreign Minister Erik Deryke is expected to discuss Zaire with his colleagues, seeking in particular some response to the increasing refugee problem.

Western nations have advised their citizens to leave Zaire. The appeals came most notably from the three countries with the greatest clout in the tormented region -- the United States, France and Belgium, the former regional colonial power.
On the Middle East, the EU ministers will discuss the appointment of a special envoy to help work for peace in the region.
They are not expected to name the envoy on Monday but to discuss some of the tasks he or she will perform.
Urged on mainly by France, the EU, the biggest financial contributor to the Middle East peace process, is keen to take a larger political role in the region.
